newsitem.title: UK: Oil dealers debate whether bull run is finished.
newsitem.headline: Oil dealers debate whether bull run is finished.

text.p: Oil prices stabilised on Friday as traders assessed the possibility of further declines in the wake of a 10-day price slide which some believe signals the end of crude's long bull run.

London March futures for bellwether Brent blend crude oil traded 19 cents barrel down at 1613 GMT after losing 77 cents on Thursday. Brent has fallen $1.50 in 10 days and is $3 below its January peak.
Dealers pointed to rising supplies of crude and heating oil inventories held by industrialised nations which now are above year-ago levels.
"There's no doubt the market's on the ropes," said Charles Gray at brokerage Prudential Bache in London.
And analysts said extra volumes of crude from all corners of the globe will be more than a match for fast-rising world demand in the months to come, putting prices under further pressure.
The West's energy watchdog, the International Energy Agency (IEA), said on Friday that it expected supplies of crude from producers outside of OPEC to rise a huge two million bpd this year.
It said the support prices found from delays in new oilfield projects at the end of last year would continue to wane as developments eventually come on stream.

"Although considerably less than expected, the growth in world oil supply in the last three months of 1996 and in January has been substantial and appears to have established strong upward trends in OPEC as well as non-OPEC production," the agency said in a monthly report.

Distillate stocks, including heating oil and diesel, in the leading industrial nations ended last year 12 million barrels higher than a year earlier, in surplus for the first time in 19 months, the IEA said.
Rising inventories have allowed U.S. refiners to take plants into early maintenance, reducing demand for crude along refinery row on the U.S. Gulf.
Imports into the United States, easily the world's biggest buyer, have dipped as a result, putting pressure on spot markets in Nigerian, North Sea and Latin American crudes.

Analysts, however, were wary of predicting a wholesale collapse in the price of crude. Refiners soon would be looking to raise gasoline output in the run-up to the early summer northern hemisphere driving season.
And world oil demand growth should post a robust 1.9 million bpd this year to 73.7 million, the IEA said.

"We really are in a demand boom which should limit the downside...but assuming we see the big rise in non-OPEC output, prices should return to the the $18-20 range by mid-year," said energy research director Mehdi Varzi at Kleinwort Benson.
